Molten
mōl'tn
a. (melted, cast from metal; rendering Hebrew massekah and mutsaq)
Old past participle of melt, from the Saxon meltan. Hebrew massekah means a poured or cast image, from nasak, to pour out — the same root as a drink offering poured to God, which makes the idolatrous casting a grim parody.

Biblical Definition

Molten describes metal melted and poured into a mould, and Scripture uses it in two directions that sit uncomfortably close together. Lawfully, it describes great works commanded for the worship of God: Solomon “made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other” (1 Kings 7:23), the great laver in which the priests washed. Unlawfully, and far more often, it names the manufacture of idols. Aaron “fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf” (Exodus 32:4), and the LORD's report of it to Moses on the mountain is blunt: “they have made them a molten image” (Deuteronomy 9:12). The sin at Sinai was not the worship of a rival god — Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD — but the worship of the true God by an image of Israel's own casting, which is the second commandment's exact concern. Isaiah exposes the absurdity of the trade: “The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold” (Isaiah 40:19) — a god that must be manufactured, plated, and then fastened down so it will not topple. Habakkuk asks the question that ends the matter: what profiteth the molten image, a teacher of lies?

Webster 1828 Definition

Melted and cast in a mould. Used of the molten sea Solomon made for the temple, and far more often of idols — the molten calf being worship of the true God by an image of Israel's own casting.

expand to see more

MOLTEN, pp. of melt, an old participle. Melted; fused by heat.

2. Made of melted metal; cast in a mould; as, a molten image.

3. Of the great laver of the temple; as, he made a molten sea, 1 Kings 7.

4. In Scripture, of idolatry; as, they have made them a molten image, Deut. 9.

5. Figuratively, of the heart failing; as, the hearts of the people melted.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 7:23 — "And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about."

Exodus 32:4 — "And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt."

Deuteronomy 9:12 — "And the LORD said unto me, Arise, get thee down quickly from hence; for thy people which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt have corrupted themselves; they are quickly turned aside out of the way which I commanded them; they have made them a molten image."

Isaiah 40:19 — "The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains."

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is imagined as a primitive matter of statues, safely behind us. The molten calf was an image of the true God made to Israel's specification, and that error is perennial.

expand to see more

The comfortable reading of Exodus 32 says Israel abandoned the LORD for a foreign deity, which lets a modern reader off. The text says otherwise: Aaron built an altar before the calf and proclaimed a feast to the LORD. The people were not swapping gods; they were worshipping the God who brought them out of Egypt by means of an image they had cast themselves, and the second commandment forbids exactly that. Idolatry in its most common biblical form is not the worship of another god but the worship of the true God in a way he has not commanded — which is why the regulative principle follows from this commandment and not merely from taste.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's mockery in 40:19, transposed to our own manufacture. A god who must be cast is a god shaped by the caster, and men still prefer a deity of their own specification — a God without wrath, or without particular election, or without the exclusivity of Christ — assembled from the attributes they find agreeable. That is a molten image with no metal in it. Habakkuk 2:18 gives the verdict: the molten image is a teacher of lies, precisely because the maker trusts in the work of his own hands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew massekah is a cast image, from nasak, to pour out — the same root as a poured drink offering. Mutsaq means cast or hard-poured, and pesel is the carved image with which massekah is often paired.

expand to see more

Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten or cast image; the calf at Sinai and the calves at Dan and Bethel.

Hebrew nasak (H5258) — to pour out, to cast metal; also used of pouring a drink offering.

Hebrew mutsaq (H3332) — cast, poured, hardened; used of the molten sea in 1 Kings 7:23.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; frequently paired with massekah in the prophets.

Greek choneuo — to cast or found metal; the Septuagint's verb for making a molten image.

Usage

"Of a lawful work for the temple: he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other (1 Kings 7:23)."

"Of the sin at Sinai: after he had made it a molten calf (Exodus 32:4)."

"Of the manufacture of gods: the workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold (Isaiah 40:19)."
